15        This action arises out of a trademark dispute between Plaintiff BBK Tobacco & 
16   Foods, LLP (“BBK”) and Defendant Central Coast Agriculture Incorporated (“CCA”). 
17   BBK manufactures, distributes, and sells smoking-related products bearing its trademarked 
18   “RAW” branding.1 (Doc. 443 at 1.) CCA markets and sells cannabis products under the 
19   “Raw Garden” brand and exclusively through California-licensed dispensaries and mobile 
20   delivery services. (Id. at 2.) BBK claims CCA infringed its RAW trademarks by producing, 
21   using, advertising, distributing, selling, and offering to sell its products under the Raw 
22   Garden brand. (Id. at 3.)                                            
23        The Court reopened summary judgment after this matter was remanded from the 
24   United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. (Docs. 466, 470.) Pending before the 
25   Court are BBK’s motion for partial-summary judgment (Doc. 478) and CCA’s motion for 
26   summary judgment (Doc. 485). The motions are fully briefed, and the Court held oral 
27   argument on February 4, 2025.                                        
28   1  BBK’s  marks  include:  “RAW,”  “RAW  ORGANIC,”  “RAW  ARTESANO,” 
    “SUPERNATURAL RAW,” “RAW CONNOISSEUR,” and “RAW BLACK.”              
1        Many of the facts have been reported at length in prior Orders. (See Docs. 151, 443.) 
2   The Court will therefore discuss relevant facts only as necessary.   
3   I.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                  
4        Summary judgment is appropriate when the evidence, viewed in the light most 
5   favorable to the non-moving party, demonstrates “that there is no genuine dispute as to any 
6   material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 
7   56(a). A genuine issue of material fact exists when “the evidence is such that a reasonable 
8   jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party,” and material facts are those “that 
9   might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, 
10   Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). At the summary judgment stage, “[t]he evidence of the 
11   non-movant is to be believed, and all justifiable inferences are to be drawn in his favor.” 
12   Id. at 255 (citation omitted); see also Jesinger v. Nev. Fed. Credit Union, 24 F.3d 1127, 
13   1131 (9th Cir. 1994) (holding that the court determines whether there is a genuine issue for 
14   trial but does not weigh the evidence or determine the truth of matters asserted). 
15        When the “parties submit cross-motions for summary judgment, each motion must 
16   be considered on its own merits.” Fair Hous. Council of Riverside Cnty. v. Riverside Two, 
17   249 F.3d 1132, 1136 (9th Cir. 2001) (citations and internal quotations omitted). The 
18   summary judgment standard operates differently depending on whether the moving or 
19   non-moving party has the burden of proof. See Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 
20   322-23 (1986). When the movant bears the burden of proof on a claim at trial, the movant 
21   “must establish beyond controversy every essential element” of the claim based on the 
22   undisputed material facts to be entitled to summary judgment. S. Cal. Gas Co. v. City of 
23   Santa Ana, 336 F.3d 885, 888 (9th Cir. 2003) (citation and internal quotations omitted). If 
24   the movant fails to make this showing, summary judgment is inappropriate, even if the 
25   non-moving party has not introduced contradictory evidence in response. When, on the 
26   other hand, the non-movant bears the burden of proof on a claim at trial, the movant may 
27   prevail either by citing evidence negating an essential element of the non-movant’s claim 
28   or by showing that the non-movant’s proffered evidence is insufficient to establish an 
1   essential element of the non-movant’s claim. See Celotex, 477 U.S. at 322-23; Nissan Fire 
2   & Marine Ins. v. Fritz Cos., 210 F.3d 1099, 1102-03 (9th Cir. 2000). 
3   II.  ANALYSIS                                                        
4        A.   CCA’s Laches and Statute of Limitations Defenses           
5        The parties both move for summary judgment on CCA’s laches and statute of 
6   limitations defenses. (Doc. 478 at 7-20; Doc. 485 at 11-17.)         
7             1.   Laches                                                
8        BBK argues that CCA’s laches affirmative defense fails because CCA cannot prove 
9   that BBK’s delay was unreasonable and prejudicial.2 (Doc. 487 at 7-18.) CCA argues that 
10   BBK’s  delay  in filing the  lawsuit  creates  a presumption  of  laches  that  BBK  cannot 
11   overcome. (Doc. 485 at 11-17.)                                       
12        “The affirmative defense of laches is an equitable time limitation on a party’s right 
13   to bring suit, which is derived from the maxim that those who sleep on their rights, lose 
14   them.” Eat Right Foods Ltd. v. Whole Foods Mkt., Inc., 880 F.3d 1109, 1115 (9th Cir. 
15   2018) (internal quotations omitted). To establish a laches defense, CCA must “prove both 
16   an unreasonable delay by the plaintiff and prejudice to itself.” See id.  
17        In trademark disputes, laches bars the claim when “the trademark holder knowingly 
18   allowed the infringing mark to be used without objection for a lengthy period of time.” Id. 
19   The Ninth Circuit makes laches determinations with reference to the statute of limitations 
20   period for the claim at issue. Id. This means that when a plaintiff files within the period, a 
21   strong presumption against laches exists, whereas if a plaintiff files outside that period the 
22   presumption is reversed. Id.                                         
23        Because the Lanham Act does not contain a statute of limitations, the Ninth Circuit 
24   presumes that Congress intended to use “the limitations period from the most closely 
25   analogous action under state law.” Jarrow Formulas, Inc. v. Nutrition Now, Inc., 304 F.3d 
26                                                                        
    2 BBK also argues that the federal illegality of CCA’s business precludes equitable relief. 
27   (Doc. 478 at 6-7.) As discussed in a prior Order, “BBK initiated this action and forced CCA 
    to defend itself. It would be manifestly unjust to preclude CCA from challenging the 
28   validity of the marks upon which BBK’s claims are based.” (Doc. 443 at 48-49.) The Court 
    finds that same reasoning applies here.                              
1   829, 836 (9th Cir. 2002). The parties here agree that the most analogous Arizona statute of 
2   limitations is three-years for fraud. (Doc. 485 at 11-12 (citing Au-Tomotive Gold Inc. v. 
3   Volkswagen of Am., Inc., 603 F.3d 1133, 1140 (9th Cir. 2010)); Doc.478 at 8); see also 
4   A.R.S. § 12-543.                                                     
5                  a.   Length of Delay                                  
6        The parties disagree as to when the laches clock started. CCA argues that the clock 
7   started in July 2016, when the parties interacted during the 2016 Chalice Cup festival. (Doc. 
8   485 at 12.) BBK argues that it could not have known that CCA’s Raw Garden brand was 
9   infringing before September 18, 2016 (three-years before the lawsuit was filed). (Doc. 478 
10   at 9.) Specifically, BBK argues that CCA was in the cannabis “services” industry rather 
11   than the cannabis “products” industry, meaning that the likelihood of confusion did not 
12   exist prior to 2018 when CCA started offering products. (Doc. 478 at 9-10.) 
13        To measure the length of the delay, courts “start the clock when the plaintiff knew 
14   (or should have known) of the allegedly infringing conduct,” and “stop it when the lawsuit 
15   in which the defendant seeks to invoke the laches defenses is initiated.” Eat Right Foods 
16   Ltd., 880 F.3d at 1116 (internal quotations omitted).                
17        CCA’s predecessors were formed in 2008 by Thomas Martin and Khalid Al-Naser 
18   when they began growing and trading cannabis for use under California’s Compassionate 
19   Use Act. (Doc. 443 at 2.) BBK and CCA (or its predecessors) have attended many of the 
20   same trade shows and competitions, including the 2016 Chalice Cup festival, a cannabis 
21   industry gathering held annually in southern California. (Id. at 2-3.) 
22        At the 2016 Chalice Cup, a BBK brand ambassador and a BBK volunteer visited 
23   CCA’s Raw Garden booth and spoke with CCA employees. (Doc. 485-14 at 17-19; Doc. 
24   485-20 at 7.) BBK’s brand ambassador, Michael D’Aquinsto, “saw a ‘Raw Garden’ booth 
25   that displayed cartridges, pre-rolls[,] and apparel,” and he also traded some of BBK’s 
26   “RAW papers for two hats with the ‘Raw Garden’ name on them, gave one hat to Rodney 
27   Peters and took the other one home.” (Doc. 485-16 at 26.) D’Aquisto gave his RAW 
28   business cards to CCA representatives and discussed potentially working together. (Doc. 
1   485-14 at 20.)                                                       
2        Afterwards, on July 16, 2016, BBK’s marketing purchasing manager, Dale Mercer, 
3   sent an email with a screenshot of CCA’s @raw_garden Instagram page to BBK’s general 
4   counsel, Brendan Mahoney. (Doc. 486-6; Doc. 485-18 at 9.) The email contains only the 
5   screenshot—no  accompanying  text—and  the  subject  line  has  been  redacted  due  to 
6   attorney-client  privilege.  (Doc.  486-6;  Doc.  485-18  at  14.)  Nonetheless,  deposition 
7   testimony from Mr. Mercer explains that “I saw that post based on my investigation and 
8   my normal process is if I think it is something that my general counsel needs to see, I am 
9   going to do it immediately so I don’t forget.” (Doc. 485-18 at 14.)  
10        Mr. Mercer also testified that he followed @dr_budz, the Instagram page of Rodney 
11   Peters, who was the BBK volunteer at the 2016 Chalice Cup and later became a BBK brand 
12   ambassador. (Doc. 485-18 at 15; Doc. 502-6 at 3.) The @dr_budz page also follows 
13   @raw_garden. (Doc. 486-6; Doc. 485-18 at 15.) Also on July 16, 2016, @dr_budz posted 
14   a photo of RAW rolling papers, cannabis, and a hat with the Raw Garden logo. (Doc. 
15   487-15.) The post is captioned “Shout out to @raw_garden for the #Slymer to roll the 
16   #rawlife247 way. Got the hat too. They are an all organic gardening for the patients. Glad 
17   we could talk at @chalicefestival using my Limited Edition . . . .” (Id.) 
18        Here, the undisputed material facts show that BBK should have known about the 
19   allegedly infringing conduct by July 16, 2016. Though the initial interactions between BBK 
20   and CCA were between marketing representatives and not executives of the company, 
21   BBK’s executives admit to knowing about CCA’s Raw Garden brand. Most importantly, 
22   Mr. Mercer felt compelled to notify Mr. Mahoney of the Raw Garden brand after the 
23   interactions from the Chalice Cup. This indicates some sort of concern. 
24        BBK claims that CCA did not break out into a related market until 2018, so it had 
25   no reason to be concerned about its Raw Garden brand until then. The Court finds this 
26   argument unpersuasive. The images from social media show that BBK staff found the 
27   products complementary in 2016. Furthermore, in 2014, CCA posted images of RAW 
28   rolling papers on social media in conjunction with Raw Garden cannabis (Docs. 496-15, 
1   496-16); see, e.g., Internet Specialties W., Inc. v. Milon-DiGiorgio Enters., Inc., 559 F.3d 
2   985, 990-91 (9th Cir. 2009) (concluding that, even though only one party initially offered 
3   DSL, both companies offered very similar services (internet, e-mail, web hosting) within 
4   the same geographic area with similar names so that defendant should have reasonably 
5   known of the alleged infringing conduct).                            
6        These undisputed facts show that BBK executives knew of the Raw Garden brand, 
7   found it significant, and as such, should have known of allegedly infringing conduct on 
8   July 16, 2016.                                                       
9                  b.   Overcoming Laches Presumption                    
10        Because BBK filed the lawsuit on September 18, 2019, more than three years after 
11   July 16, 2016, the presumption of laches applies. See Eat Right Foods Ltd., 880 F.3d at 
12   1115. BBK can overcome this presumption if it “can show that its delay in suing was 
13   nonetheless reasonable.” See id. at 1117; La Quinta Worldwide LLC v. Q.R.T.M., S.A. de 
14   C.V., 762 F.3d 867, 878 (9th Cir. 2014).                             
15        Courts use the following factors from E-Systems, Inc. v. Monitek, Inc., 720 F.2d 604 
16   (9th Cir. 1983), to determine whether a plaintiff’s delay in bring the case was unreasonable 
17   and barred by laches:                                                
18             1. strength and value of trademark rights asserted;        
19             2. plaintiff’s diligence in enforcing mark;                
20             3. harm to senior user if relief denied;                   
21             4. good faith ignorance by junior user;                    
22             5. competition between senior and junior users; and        
23             6. extent of harm suffered by junior user because of senior 
              user’s delay.                                              
24                                                                        
25   La Quinta, 762 F.3d at 878; Internet Specialties, 559 F.3d at 991.   
26        BBK argues that the Ninth Circuit’s mandate impacts analysis for the strength and 
27   value of the trademark rights (factor 1) and harm to senior user (factor 3). The Court 
28   previously found the RAW mark is “likely descriptive and at most suggestive.” (Doc. 443 
1   at 34.) As for the harm to the senior user, this factor “turns largely on the court’s analysis 
2   of the likelihood of confusion.” Fitbug Ltd. v. Fitbit, Inc., 78 F. Supp. 3d 1180, 1193 (N.D. 
3   Cal. 2015). The Court previously found no likelihood of confusion between the RAW mark 
4   and Raw Garden. (Doc. 443 at 25, 44.) The Ninth Circuit, however, found that BBK raised 
5   material issues of fact regarding the strength of the marks and likelihood of confusion under 
6   the Sleekcraft factors. (Doc. 466-1 at 3.) Regardless, even assuming these factors weigh in 
7   favor  of  unreasonable  delay,  the  undisputed  material  facts  show  that  the  remaining 
8   E-System factors weight in favor of BBK—meaning, the delay was reasonable. 
9        The Court finds BBK was diligent in enforcing its RAW mark (factor 2). The delay 
10   in filing the lawsuit outside the statute of limitations is less than three-months. Also, the 
11   undisputed facts show that BBK tried to defend its mark within the three-years after July 
12   16, 2016.                                                            
13        On April 17, 2017, BBK received a trademark watch notice indicating that CCA 
14   filed a U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (“USPTO”) application with its intent to use the 
15   “Raw Garden” mark. (Doc. 229-2 at 8 ¶ 28, 166-67.) On April 25, 2017, BBK filed a letter 
16   of  protest  for  CCA’s  application  claiming  a  notification  of  prior  registrations  and  a 
17   likelihood of confusion with BBK’s RAW mark. (Doc. 229-2 at 175-77.) The USPTO 
18   approved CCA’s application on December 27, 2017, and published the CCA application 
19   for opposition on January 16, 2018. (Doc. 229-2 at 166-67.) That same day, BBK filed 
20   with the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board a request for a 90-day extension to oppose the 
21   Raw  Garden  application.  (Id.;  id.  at  179.)  The  parties  then  engaged  in  settlement 
22   negotiations from May 31, 2018, to December 20, 2018.3 (Doc. 229-2 at 9 ¶ 35; Doc. 
23   418-1.) This short delay along with the parties’ settlement negotiation alone can be enough 
24   to overcome the laches presumption. See Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc. v. Tabari, 610 
25   F.3d 1171, 1183 (9th Cir. 2010) (holding district court did not abuse its discretion after 

26   3 CCA does not dispute that settlement discussions occurred during this timeline. (See Doc. 
    502  at  13-14.)  CCA,  however,  objects  to  the  summary  exhibit  of  settlement 
27   communications (Doc. 418-1) as insufficiently voluminous, inadmissible  hearsay and 
    lacking proper foundational documentation. (Doc. 502 at 14 n.7.) The Court, however, does 
28   not use this exhibit for the truth of the matter asserted (i.e., the content of the settlement 
    negotiations), but rather, to show that settlement discussions occurred during 2018. 
1   finding a two-year delay reasonable, barring laches, because the parties were actively 
2   engaged in settlement negotiations); Eat Right Foods, 880 F.3d at 1118-19 (remanding 
3   laches claim back to the district court after finding a material disputed fact as to whether 
4   the plaintiff’s delay was reasonable if the parties were actively engaged in settlement 
5   negations).                                                          
6        For similar reasons, the Court finds that CCA did not suffer harm because of BBK’s 
7   short delay of three months (factor 6). CCA claims that it suffers evidentiary prejudice 
8   because of the delay in filing the lawsuit. Allegedly, because of the delay, various witnesses 
9   (including BBK witnesses) do not remember the facts from the past. (Doc. 485 at 16.) The 
10   Court finds this unpersuasive. If BBK filed the lawsuit three months earlier, within the 
11   three-year statute of limitations, the laches presumption would fail, and the parties would 
12   likely still experience the same minimal degree of memory degradation. CCA also claims 
13   that  it  experiences  expectation-based  prejudice  because  it  thought  it  had  a  cordial 
14   relationship with BBK—that CCA would not have invested in the Raw Garden brand had 
15   it known BBK opposed it. (Id.) Yet, the undisputed facts show that BBK opposed the use 
16   of the Raw Garden mark as early as April 27, 2017, when it filed its letter with the USPTO.  
17        The Court also finds the factors of good faith ignorance by CCA (factor 4) and 
18   competition between BBK and CCA (factor 5) weigh in favor of BBK. CCA claims that 
19   no evidence exists that CCA “sought to free-ride on [BBK’s] good will or otherwise take 
20   unfair advantage of the similarity between the two companies’ marks.” (Doc. 485 at 15 
21   quoting Pinkette Clothing, Inc. v. Cosm. Warriors Ltd., 894 F.3d 1015, 1028 (9th Cir. 
22   2018).) See also Fitbug, 78 F. Supp. 3d at 1194 (finding good faith ignorance factor 
23   considers whether the defendant had prior knowledge of the plaintiff’s mark before it 
24   decided to adopt the name). CCA claims that BBK and CCA are not competitors because 
25   CCA’s  products  contain  cannabis,  while  none  of  BBK’s  products  do,  and  that  its 
26   merchandise is merely incidental to CCA’s brand. (Doc. 485 at 15.) Undisputed facts show, 
27   however, that CCA knew of the RAW brand and that the Raw Garden products are 
28   complementary to BBK’s RAW brand. John De Friel, CCA’s chief executive officer, knew 
1   of BBK’s RAW branded rolling papers since 2005 (Doc. 496-14 at 4), and in 2014, CCA 
2   and others posted images of RAW rolling papers on social media in conjunction with Raw 
3   Garden cannabis (Docs. 496-15, 496-16). CCA also reached out to BBK in 2017 about the 
4   possibility of the RAW branded cones being printed with “Raw Garden.” (Doc. 485-20 at 
5   20-24.) Furthermore, CCA even notes in its papers that the Court previously found that 
6   some  of  BBK’s  products  use  the  RAW  mark  on  of  its  “federally-illegal  drug 
7   paraphernalia”—another complementary product. (Doc. 502 at 8 n.1.)   
8        On balance, the Court finds the undisputed material facts show that the E-System 
9   factors weight in favor of BBK and show that the delay was reasonable. As such, laches 
10   does not bar BBK’s trademark claims.                                 
11        Therefore, with respect to the laches defense, the Court grants BBK’s motion 
12   (Doc. 478 at 7-18) and denies CCA’s motion (Doc. 485 at 11-17).      
13             2.   Statute of Limitations                                
14        BBK  and  CCA  both  move  for  summary  judgment  on  whether  the  statute  of 
15   limitations ran on BBK’s Arizona common law infringement and unfair competition 
16   claims. (Doc. 478 at 19-20; Doc. 485 at 17.)                         
17        Both claims are subject to a three-year statute of limitations. See Ranch Realty, Inc. 
18   v. DC Ranch Realty, LLC, 614 F. Supp. 2d 983, 989-90 (D. Ariz. 2007). Yet, under the 
19   doctrine of continuing tort, “a tort claim based on a series of related wrongful acts is 
20   considered continuous, and accrual begins at the termination of the wrongdoing, rather than 
21   at the beginning.” Crus v. City of Tucson, 243 Ariz. 69, 74 (App. 2017). 
22        Here, the fact that BBK did not file the claims until September 18, 2019, outside the 
23   three-year statute of limitations, does not preclude BBK’s state-law claims in their entirety. 
24   See 4 McCarthy on Trademarks and Unfair Competition § 31:33 (4th ed.) (“Usually, 
25   infringement is a continuing wrong, and the statute of limitations is no bar except as to 
26   damages beyond the statutory period.”). Rather, the claims are limited to the three-years 
27   preceding the filing of the lawsuit. See, e.g., Novell, Inc. v. Unicom Sales, Inc., No. C-03-
28   2785 MMC, 2004 WL 1839117, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 17, 2004).          
1        Therefore, with respect to statute of limitations, the Court grants BBK’s motion 
2   (Doc. 478 at 19-20) and denies CCA’s motion (Doc. 485 at 17) as a matter of law. BBK’s 
3   Arizona  common  law  infringement  and  unfair  competition  claims  are  limited  to  the 
4   three-year time period before September 18, 2019.                    
5        B.   CCA’s Other Defenses                                       
6        BBK moves for summary judgment on CCA’s remaining affirmative defenses 
7   (1) acquiescence, (2) waiver, (3) estoppel, (4) unclean hands, and (5) other defenses. 
8             1.   Acquiescence                                          
9        “Acquiescence, as a defense to trademark infringement, requires that (1) the senior 
10   user actively represented that it would not assert a right or a claim, (2) the delay between 
11   the active representation and assertion of the right or claim was not excusable, and (3) the 
12   delay caused the defendant undue prejudice.” PetConnect Rescue, Inc. v. Salinas, 656 F. 
13   Supp.  3d  1131,  1180  (S.D.  Cal.  2023)  (emphasis  added).  Acquiescence  requires  an 
14   affirmative word or deed conveying consent to use the trademark. Seller Agency Council, 
15   Inc. v. Kennedy Ctr. for Real Est. Educ., Inc., 621 F.3d 981, 988-89 (9th Cir. 2010). 
16        For similar reasons that the laches defense fails, the Court finds CCA’s acquiescence 
17   defense must also fail. As discussed, no evidence suggests that BBK actively represented 
18   it would not assert its right in the RAW mark. In fact, BBK contested CCA’s use of Raw 
19   Garden with the USPTO in 2017. Also, as discussed, the Court found the three-month delay 
20   in filing the lawsuit reasonable.                                    
21        The Court therefore grants BBK’s motion (Doc. 478 at 18) with respect to the 
22   acquiescence defense.                                                
23             2.   Waiver                                                
24        “A waiver is an intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right or 
25   privilege.” United States v. Amwest Sur. Ins. Co., 54 F.3d 601, 602 (9th Cir. 1995) (citation 
26   omitted). The “waiver must be manifested in an unequivocal manner.” Monster Energy Co. 
27   v. BeastUp LLC, 395 F. Supp. 3d 1334, 1367 (E.D. Cal. 2019). “An implied waiver of 
28   rights  will  be found where there is ‘clear, decisive and unequivocal’ conduct which 
1   indicates a purpose to waive the legal rights involved.” Amwest Sur. Ins. Co., 54 F.3d at 
2   602-03.                                                              
3        CCA presents evidence that BBK representatives (1) learned of the Raw Garden at 
4   the 2016 Chalice Cup festival and discussed potential collaboration because each had the 
5   word “Raw” in their name and exchanged merchandise and business cards (Doc. 485-14 at 
6   18-20) and (2) made social media posts “shout[ing] out to @raw_garden” (Doc. 486-7). 
7   CCA also contacted BBK for pricing of the RAW rolling papers because “we had had a 
8   positive interaction with one of their reps at [the] Chalice [Cup] the year before.” (Doc. 
9   485-20 at 7.)                                                        
10        BBK argues that there is no evidence in the record of a  “clear, decisive and 
11   unequivocal” manifestation of its intent to relinquish any of its trademark rights. (Doc. 478 
12   at 19.)                                                              
13        Viewing these facts in the light most favorable to CCA, these actions do not show 
14   a material disputed fact that BBK expressed “clear, decisive and unequivocal conduct” to 
15   relinquish or abandon its trademark rights. Nothing about BBK’s behavior is decisive or 
16   clear, and these actions are not from BBK executives, but people who work in marketing. 
17   There is no evidence that these marketing employees had any authority to make decisions 
18   impacting BBK’s legal rights. To the contrary, as discussed, BBK opposed CCA’s 2017 
19   application to the USPTO—showing BBK’s intent to defend its trademark rights. See, e.g., 
20   Monster Energy Co., 395 F. Supp. 3d at 1367 (finding the defendant provided no evidence 
21   of “clear, decisive and unequivocal” conduct and that the plaintiff sought to enforce its 
22   rights).                                                             
23        The Court therefore grants BBK’s motion (Doc. 478 at 19) with respect to CCA’s 
24   waiver defense.                                                      
25             3.   Estoppel                                              
26        “Unlike waiver, estoppel focuses not on a party’s intent, but rather on the effects of 
27   his conduct on another. Estoppel arises only when a party’s conduct misleads another to 
28   believe that a right will not be enforced and causes him to act to his detriment in reliance 
1   upon this belief.” adidas-America, Inc. v. Payless Shoesource, Inc., 546 F. Supp. 2d 1029, 
2   1075 (D.  Or.  2008).  CCA  must  prove:  (1)  BBK  knew  CCA  was  selling  potentially 
3   infringing cannabis products and merchandise; (2) BBK’s actions or failure to act led CCA 
4   to reasonably believe that BBK did not intend to enforce its trademark right against CCA; 
5   (3) CCA did not know that BBK actually objected to the sale of its potentially infringing 
6   products; and (4) due to its reliance on BBK’s actions, CCA will be materially prejudiced 
7   if BBK is allowed to proceed with its claim. See id.                 
8        Here, viewing the facts in favor of CCA, the Court finds that BBK’s actions did not 
9   lead CCA to reasonably believe that BBK did not intend to enforce its trademark rights 
10   against CAA. The undisputed facts show that BBK opposed the use of the Raw Garden 
11   mark as early as April 27, 2017, when it filed its letter with the USPTO. 
12        The Court therefore grants BBK’s motion (Doc. 478 at 19) with respect to CCA’s 
13   estoppel defense.                                                    
14             4.   Unclean Hands                                         
15        BBK argues, in part, that CCA ignored the Court’s Scheduling Order (Doc. 31) and 
16   improperly  injected  a  new  unclean  hands  affirmative  defense  in  its  third  MIDP 
17   supplemental disclosures from September 5, 2024. (Doc. 478 at 20; Doc. 478-25.) In 
18   essence, BBK wants the Court to preclude CCA from presenting evidence that may be 
19   improperly disclosed—a sanction under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(c)(1). BBK, 
20   however, does not brief the issue under the Rule 37(c)(1) standard.  
21        The Court finds this argument regarding improper disclosure better suited for a 
22   motion in limine before trial, rather than a motion for summary judgment. In the motion in 
23   limine, the parties can address the appropriate Rule 37(c)(1) standard, including whether 
24   the alleged late disclosure “was substantially justified or is harmless.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 
25   37(c)(1); Liberty Ins. Corp. v. Brodeur, 41 F.4th 1185, 1191-92 (9th Cir. 2022). 
26        The Court therefore denies BBK’s motion (Doc. 478 at 20-22) with respect to 
27   CCA’s unclean hands defense.                                         
28                                                                        
1             5.   Other Defenses                                        
2        BBK  argues  that  CCA’s  first,  second,  seventh,  tenth,  eleventh,  and  thirteenth 
3   affirmative defenses are not affirmative defenses because CCA does not meet its burden of 
4   proof. (Doc. 478 at 22.)                                             
5        The Court finds that BBK has not met its burden as the moving party that summary

24   customers  from  the  mark  owner’s  online  location . . . by  creating  a  likelihood  of

27   registered after the defendant became aware of its mark. (Doc. 496 at 18.) Specifically, 
28   BBK relies on an interrogatory response explaining that Mr. De Friel became aware of 
1   RAW branded rolling papers in or around 2005 while visiting a smoke shop in Seattle. 
2   (Doc. 496-14 at 4.) This evidence is insufficient when compared to the cases cited by BBK.

202 F.3d 489
, 499
